name: Genotropin

lead: Genotropin is the brand name of a recombinant human growth hormone (somatropin) made by Pfizer, formerly Pharmacia. It is prescribed for children with growth hormone deficiency, Turner syndrome, Prader-Willi syndrome, chronic renal insufficiency and short stature from being born small for gestational age.

Its appearance connection is height and body composition. Clinical trials measure how much faster children grow while treated, and forum users in height and bodybuilding communities discuss using brand-name growth hormone for height or leanness. Trial evidence applies to children with open growth plates.

paras: Under prescription, Genotropin is given by injection under the skin on a schedule set by a pediatric or adult endocrinologist, with growth and hormone levels monitored. Forum threads describe non-prescription use, usually via the gray market; this article does not cover dosing or sourcing. Treatment of children runs for years, and height response is tracked against growth charts.

Documented effects of growth hormone therapy include reduced insulin sensitivity, and clinicians monitor for other effects. Regulators and endocrinology bodies caution about use outside approved indications, and counterfeit or mislabeled products circulate on gray markets. Genotropin is a prescription-only drug in the US, UK and EU.

angle.text: In children with open growth plates and a diagnosed growth condition, Genotropin raises annual growth in trials. Forum users also discuss it for height and lean body composition outside medical supervision.

lead: Genotropin is a brand of recombinant human growth hormone (somatropin) marketed by Pfizer, which inherited it from Pharmacia, itself the successor of the Swedish company Kabi that had sold the first commercial growth hormone product in the late 1970s [1][2][3]. It is one of several recombinant products, alongside Humatrope, Norditropin, Nutropin, Saizen and Zomacton, and it is the only growth hormone with an FDA indication for children with Prader-Willi syndrome [2][3].

For appearance, its relevance is height and body composition. In pediatric endocrinology the hormone is prescribed to increase growth velocity in children whose growth has been limited by deficiency or by conditions such as Turner syndrome or being born small for gestational age [4][5]. Online communities concerned with height and physique also discuss it, as a pharmaceutical-grade product compared with cheaper generic hGH [6][7].

Research on Genotropin includes randomized trials in children born small for gestational age, trials in idiopathic short stature, and active-comparator studies in which new long-acting growth hormones are compared with daily Genotropin [8][9][10].

In height and bodybuilding forums the brand has a reputation as the premium pen-delivered hGH, and threads compare its price per international unit with cheaper generic products and ask whether it can add height or leanness outside medical care [6][7][11]. Endocrinology journals, the FDA and the Endocrine Society have commented separately on use in healthy people and in idiopathic short stature, summarised below [2].

paras: Genotropin is licensed for children with growth hormone deficiency, Prader-Willi syndrome, Turner syndrome, chronic renal insufficiency and those born small for gestational age [5]. Studies in Prader-Willi syndrome also report effects on body composition and physical strength in children, and adult studies are fewer [12].

The appearance goals described in community threads are added height and a leaner, more muscular body [6][7]. Questions typically compare the brand-name product with generic hGH from other manufacturers.

Before recombinant technology, human growth hormone could only be obtained from human pituitary glands. Pig and cow hormone does not work in people. In the late 1950s Maurice Raben purified enough human pituitary hormone to treat a deficient boy, and in 1960 the US National Pituitary Agency began collecting glands at autopsy for distribution. Roughly 7,700 US children and 27,000 children worldwide received pituitary-derived hormone between 1963 and 1985 [2].

In the late 1970s the Swedish company Kabi began buying pituitaries to make Crescormon, the first commercial growth hormone product. In 1981 Genentech, working with Kabi, began trials of biosynthetic hormone [2]. In 1985 four young American adults who had been treated in the 1960s developed Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and pituitary-derived hormone was withdrawn; Wikipedia reports 26 cases among recipients between 1985 and 2003, none among those given only hormone made by the improved 1977 method [2]. The FDA approved Genentech's recombinant Protropin the same year [2].

Competing recombinant products followed from Eli Lilly (Humatrope), Novo (Norditropin), Serono, Ferring and Pharmacia, whose Kabi line became Genotropin and later passed to Pfizer [2][3]. The products differ mainly in formulation and delivery device [2]. Genotropin was also used as the active comparator in the first trials of long-acting once-weekly hormones, such as the 2022 Japanese somatrogon study [10], and the FDA approved the first once-weekly product, somapacitan, in 2020 [2].

sections.h: Indications and the idiopathic short stature debate
paras: Approved pediatric uses of growth hormone as a class include deficiency, Turner syndrome, chronic kidney failure, SHOX deficiency, being born small for gestational age and Prader-Willi syndrome; Wikipedia reports median adult height gain in Turner syndrome of about 5 to 8 cm [2]. Genotropin is the only product with an FDA indication for Prader-Willi syndrome, and only in children [2][3].

Idiopathic short stature, in which a child is very short without an identified hormonal cause, is a more debated indication. Pediatric endocrinologists disagree about its definition. In late-1990s Eli Lilly trials, children at least 2.25 standard deviations below the mean height gained roughly 4 to 8 cm in adult height, and critics questioned whether the children were simply short but normal. The FDA approved Humatrope for the indication in 2003, after which more parents sought treatment to make otherwise healthy children taller [2]. A four-year randomized Genotropin study in idiopathic short stature compared individualized and standard regimens [9].

A 2010 systematic review for a UK health technology appraisal found 30 randomized trials of Genotropin in children but only one reporting final height, plus eleven observational studies with final-height data, many drawn from the Pfizer International Growth Survey (KIGS); the authors called for long-term trials reporting final height [5].

In a two-year randomized study in very young children born small for gestational age, the treated group's height standard deviation score rose by 1.63 versus 0.43 in the untreated group [8]. A four-year randomized study compared individualized with standard Genotropin dosing in idiopathic short stature [9].

In a Japanese phase 3 trial in children with growth hormone deficiency, once-weekly somatrogon was compared with daily Genotropin over 12 months, with annualized height velocity of 9.65 versus 7.87 cm per year [10]. A 2023 meta-analysis found long-acting preparations generally comparable to daily products, including Genotropin as comparator [4].

A summary of growth hormone therapy notes that treatment usually reduces insulin sensitivity, and that a 2011 FDA communication described evidence on mortality as inconclusive [1]. A large observational cohort, the full KIGS database, has examined safety and efficacy of pediatric therapy [13]. Journal editorials have cautioned about off-label use in healthy people [1].

Wikipedia's summary adds that a study of 6,840 adults found no overall rise in primary cancer risk over relatively short follow-up, with higher risk in some subgroups, including the US cohort under 35 and people with childhood-onset deficiency [2]. Elevated mortality was reported in the critically ill [2]. Pharmaceutical products are single-use, refrigerated biologics; forum posts raise counterfeit concerns about branded products, which makes provenance a safety issue [14].

For adults, the Endocrine Society's 2011 guideline recommends individualized replacement for people with hypothalamic or pituitary disease, prior pituitary surgery or radiation, or head trauma, and says idiopathic adult deficiency is very rare and needs stringent testing. Reported benefits of replacement include higher bone density, more muscle and less fat [2].

Interest in healthy adults grew after Daniel Rudman's widely publicized 1990 trial in men over 60 and a 1997 book by Ronald Klatz promoting the hormone for anti-aging [2]. In 2003 New England Journal of Medicine editorials by Jeffrey Drazen and Mary Lee Vance cautioned that safety and efficacy had not been shown in healthy or elderly adults and that long-term risks were unknown [2]. A 1999 study by Takala and colleagues found higher mortality in critically ill adults given hormone [2]. In 2011 the FDA stated that evidence on increased mortality was inconclusive [2]. Wikipedia also notes that products sold online under the label HGH include many that are not pharmaceutical somatropin [2].

Threads on looksmax.org discuss Genotropin versus generic hGH, whether to pair it with IGF-1 LR3, and purchase prices of pens [6][7][11]. T Nation members have described using pharmaceutical-grade growth hormone alongside other compounds for physique goals [15]. Because this involves prescription drugs, the wiki does not reproduce dosing or sourcing information.
Forum users and other communities discuss counterfeit risk and authentication of branded growth hormone products [14].

Randomized and observational studies of Genotropin in children cover growth hormone deficiency, small for gestational age, idiopathic short stature and Prader-Willi syndrome, with outcomes measured as height velocity and height standard deviation score [5][8][9][10][12][4]. These studies enrolled children with open growth plates; none studied non-prescription use for height in healthy adults.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org and T Nation, Genotropin is discussed as a premium brand of growth hormone, mostly in questions about height, cost and how it compares with generics [6][7][15]. Questions typically concern price per unit, authenticity of pens and whether adults can still gain height [6][7][14].

Kabi begins commercial pituitary-derived growth hormone production (Crescormon) [2].
Genentech, working with Kabi, begins trials of recombinant human growth hormone [2].
Pituitary-derived hormone withdrawn after Creutzfeldt-Jakob cases; Genentech's Protropin approved; competing brands including Pharmacia's Genotropin follow [1][1][2].
Rudman trial in older men draws public interest in growth hormone for aging [2].
FDA approves Humatrope for idiopathic short stature; NEJM editorials caution on off-label use [2].
